title: How Claude Code works
blurb: Before any configuration makes sense, you need the mental model: what a session is, what Claude can see, and who decides what runs.

lessons.title: What Claude Code actually is
lessons.objective: Describe the agent loop and say what makes Claude Code different from a chat window.
lessons.teach:
Claude Code is an agent that runs on your machine. You describe a goal in plain English; it reads files, runs commands, and edits code to get there, then reports back. That loop — think, act, observe, repeat — is the whole product.

The difference from a chat window is that it acts on real state. A chat assistant returns text you then apply yourself. Claude Code applies it. That is why almost everything else you will learn is about constraining what it may do, rather than about getting better answers.

One turn looks like this:

  1. You send a prompt.
  2. Claude decides on a tool call — read this file, run this command, edit that function.
  3. The harness — the Claude Code program itself, not the model — decides whether that call is allowed. It may run it, block it, or ask you.
  4. The result goes back to Claude, which decides on the next call, or stops and answers.

Hold on to step 3. The model proposes; the harness disposes. Every permission rule, hook and sandbox setting in this course is you programming step 3.

example.label: The surfaces it runs on
example.code:
claude                    # interactive terminal session
claude -p "fix the test"   # one-shot, non-interactive (scripts, CI)

# also: VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app,
# claude.ai/code on the web, GitHub Actions, and a Slack integration.

lessons.takeaway: Claude proposes tool calls; the harness decides whether they run. Configuration is how you program that decision.

checks.q: You add a rule that blocks a command. Claude still tries to run it. Is that a failure?
choices: Yes — the rule should stop Claude from trying
No — Claude proposes tool calls and the harness blocks them; a blocked attempt is the system working
Yes — it means the rule syntax is wrong
Only if it happens more than once
checks.why: Rules act on the harness, not on Claude's intentions. Claude may well propose a blocked call; the block is what makes the rule real. This is why enforcement lives in rules and hooks rather than in instructions you write in prose.

lessons.title: The context window
lessons.objective: Say what is loaded before you type, and why context is the scarce resource.
lessons.teach:
Claude has no memory between sessions. Everything it knows about your project arrives in the context window — a finite budget of tokens holding the system prompt, your instructions, the conversation, and every file it has read.

Before you type a single character, a session has already loaded:

  • the system prompt (~4k tokens) — core instructions you never see
  • auto memory — notes Claude wrote itself in past sessions
  • environment info — working directory, platform, shell, plus git branch and status as a separate block
  • your CLAUDE.md files and any unscoped rules
  • tool definitions, and the names of MCP tools

Two consequences follow, and they drive a lot of later design:

Context is spent, not free. A 400-line CLAUDE.md costs its tokens on every single turn, forever. That is the argument for moving long procedures into skills, which load only when used.

Reading files is the main cost. A search that opens forty files can consume more window than the entire rest of your session. That is the argument for subagents, which do the reading in a separate window and hand back only the conclusion.

example.label: Inspect your own session
example.code:
/context     # visualize what is in the window right now
/compact     # summarize the history, keep working
/clear       # throw the history away and start fresh

lessons.takeaway: Everything Claude knows is in one finite window. Context is the budget you are always spending.

checks.q: You finish one task and start a completely unrelated one in the same session. /clear or /compact?
choices: /clear — the task changed, so the old history is pure cost
checks.why: /compact summarizes and continues, which is right when the same task got long. When the task itself changed, that history has no future value — it is just tokens you keep paying for. /clear is correct.

checks.q: Why does reading many files hurt more than a long prompt?
choices: File contents are billed at a higher rate
File contents stay in the window for the rest of the session, so their cost repeats every turn
It does not — they cost the same
checks.why: Once read, a file's contents sit in the conversation and are re-sent with every subsequent turn. A one-off long prompt is paid once; forty files are paid over and over. This is precisely the problem subagents solve.

lessons.title: Permission prompts
lessons.objective: Predict which actions prompt you, and know what 'don't ask again' actually writes.
lessons.teach:
In the default mode — called Manual — Claude Code starts read-only and asks before it changes anything. The rough shape:

  • Never prompts: reading files, Grep, Glob, and a built-in set of read-only shell commands like ls, cat and git status.
  • Prompts: editing or writing files, and any other shell command.

There is also a working directory boundary. Claude Code writes only inside the folder you started it in and below. In Manual mode it even asks before reading outside that boundary.

When you answer a prompt with “Yes, and don't ask again”, that is not a vague preference. Claude Code writes a concrete allow rule into .claude/settings.local.json — a real file, in your project, that you can open and edit. Understanding that file is the bridge to the next module.

One detail that surprises people: that file is read from the repository root, even if you started Claude Code in a subdirectory. So an approval you give in src/api/ applies across the whole repo.

example.label: What 'don't ask again' writes

lessons.takeaway: Manual mode is read-only by default. 'Don't ask again' writes a real allow rule to .claude/settings.local.json.

checks.q: Which of these run WITHOUT a prompt in Manual mode?
checks.why: A built-in read-only command set — ls, cat, git status, git diff, grep, find — runs without asking. Edits prompt, arbitrary commands prompt, and network commands like curl and wget are specifically NOT auto-approved.

lessons.title: CLAUDE.md — telling Claude about your project
lessons.objective: Know what belongs in CLAUDE.md, where it lives, and why it is not enforcement.
lessons.teach:
CLAUDE.md is a plain markdown file of standing instructions, loaded into context at the start of every session. It is where you write down what you would otherwise re-explain: build commands, conventions, project layout, “always do X” rules.

It can live in several places, loaded broadest-first:

  • Managed policy — deployed by your organization, cannot be excluded
  • User — ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, all your projects
  • Project — ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, committed for the team
  • Local — ./CLAUDE.local.md, yours, gitignored

Files are concatenated, not overridden, ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory — so the instructions closest to where you launched are read last.

Now the most important sentence in this lesson:

CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration. Claude reads it and tries to follow it. There is no guarantee, especially for vague or conflicting instructions.

So “always run the linter before committing” in CLAUDE.md is a hope. If it truly must happen every time, it belongs in a hook — which you will meet in Module 3. Keep CLAUDE.md for facts, under about 200 lines, and specific: “Use 2-space indentation” beats “format code properly”.

example.label: A CLAUDE.md that earns its tokens
example.code:
# payments-api

## Commands
- `make test` — full suite (needs a local Redis)
- `make lint` — ruff + mypy, run before committing

## Layout
- API handlers live in `src/api/handlers/`
- Anything touching money goes through `src/ledger/` — never write to
  the balances table directly

## Conventions
- 2-space indentation, no tabs
- New endpoints need a test in `tests/api/` before review

lessons.takeaway: CLAUDE.md is loaded every session and is guidance, not enforcement. Facts here; procedures in skills; guarantees in hooks.

checks.q: You put 'always run make lint before committing' in CLAUDE.md and Claude sometimes forgets. What is the structural fix?
choices: Move it to a hook — CLAUDE.md is context, not enforcement
checks.why: No amount of emphasis makes context into enforcement. An instruction tied to a specific moment — before every commit, after each edit — belongs in a hook, which the harness executes as code regardless of what Claude decides.

checks.q: You have CLAUDE.md at the repo root and another in src/api/. You launch Claude Code in src/api/. What happens?
choices: Only src/api/CLAUDE.md loads — the nearest wins
Both load, concatenated, with the root file first and src/api/ last
They conflict and Claude Code errors
checks.why: All discovered files are concatenated rather than overriding each other, ordered from the filesystem root down to your working directory. Instructions closest to where you launched are read last.

title: Controlling what Claude can do
blurb: The permission system is the densest examinable area and the one where intuition is most often wrong. Take it slowly.

lessons.title: deny → ask → allow
lessons.objective: State the evaluation order and predict the outcome when rules overlap.
lessons.teach:
You write permission rules in a settings file under three lists: deny, ask and allow. When Claude proposes a tool call, the harness checks them in a fixed order:

deny → ask → allow

The first match in that order wins, and specificity is irrelevant. This is the single most tested fact in the whole syllabus, and it is the opposite of how CSS, firewall rules, and most things programmers know actually work.

Concretely: you have Bash(aws *) in deny and Bash(aws s3 ls) in allow. Claude proposes aws s3 ls. The deny list is checked first, it matches, and the call is blocked — even though your allow rule is far more specific.

A deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions. If you need “block all of X except Y”, deny rules alone cannot express it. You will learn the technique that can in Module 3.

The same asymmetry holds between ask and allow: a matching ask rule prompts you even when a more specific allow rule also matches.

One more distinction. A bare tool name in deny behaves differently from a scoped rule:

  • deny: Bash — removes the tool from Claude's context entirely. It never sees that the tool exists.
  • deny: Bash(rm *) — the tool stays available; matching calls are blocked when attempted.

example.label: Reading a config the way the harness does

lessons.takeaway: deny → ask → allow, first match wins, specificity never breaks the tie.

checks.q: deny has Bash(aws *). allow has Bash(aws s3 ls). Claude proposes `aws s3 ls`. What happens?
choices: It runs — the allow rule is more specific
It is blocked — deny is evaluated first and specificity does not matter
You are prompted to break the tie
Claude Code reports a configuration conflict
checks.why: Rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match in that order determines the outcome. A broad deny blocks everything it matches, so a deny rule can never carry an allowlist exception.

checks.q: What does `deny: Bash` do that `deny: Bash(rm *)` does not?
choices: It removes the tool from Claude's context entirely, so Claude never sees it
It applies only in bypassPermissions mode
It blocks the tool for subagents only
checks.why: A bare tool name in deny removes the tool from Claude's context. A scoped rule leaves the tool available and blocks only matching calls. (One exception: EndConversation cannot be removed while any other tool remains.)

lessons.title: Bash rule syntax
lessons.objective: Write a Bash allow rule that matches what you intend and nothing more.
lessons.teach:
Bash rule wildcards look like shell globs and are not. Three mechanics decide everything.

1. A space before the trailing * creates a word boundary.

RuleMatchesDoes not match
Bash(ls *)ls -lalsof
Bash(ls*)ls -la and lsof—

Miss that space and you have silently widened your allowlist to every command starting with those letters. Bash(ls:*) is an equivalent way to write the word-boundary form.

2. Shell operators split the command, and every part must match independently. The recognised separators are &&, ||, ;, |, |&, & and newlines. So Bash(safe-cmd *) does not approve safe-cmd && rm -rf /. This is a deliberate defence, and it is why you cannot smuggle a command past a prefix rule.

3. A fixed list of wrappers is stripped before matching. timeout, time, nice, nohup, stdbuf, the builtins command and builtin, zsh's noglob, and bare xargs. So Bash(npm test *) also covers timeout 30 npm test.

And here is the trap. Environment runners are not stripped — npx, docker exec, devbox run, direnv exec, mise exec. Which means Bash(devbox run *) matches devbox run rm -rf .. Write one rule per inner command instead: Bash(devbox run npm test).

Finally, some things can never be prefix-approved: the exec wrappers watch, setsid, ionice, flock, and find with -exec or -delete. They always prompt in Manual mode.

example.label: Narrow rules that hold

lessons.takeaway: The space before * is a word boundary; shell operators split the command; environment runners are not stripped.

checks.q: Your allow rule is Bash(ls *). Which commands does it match?
choices: Neither — a trailing wildcard is invalid in allow
checks.why: A '*' at the end preceded by a space enforces a word boundary: the prefix must be followed by a space or end-of-string. Written without the space, Bash(ls*) matches both.

checks.q: You allow Bash(devbox run *). Why is that dangerous?
choices: devbox is not a real command
Environment runners are not stripped before matching, so the rule matches `devbox run rm -rf .`
It is not dangerous — the runner sandboxes what it runs
checks.why: The wrapper-stripping list is fixed and does not include environment runners like devbox, npx, docker exec, direnv exec or mise exec. Because these execute their arguments as a command, a prefix rule covering the runner covers anything you can pass it. Write one rule per inner command.

checks.q: With Bash(safe-cmd *) allowed, Claude proposes `safe-cmd && rm -rf /tmp/x`. What happens?
choices: It runs — the rule matched the start
It is not auto-approved; each subcommand must match a rule independently
Claude Code rejects the rule at startup
checks.why: Claude Code is aware of shell operators. It splits on &&, ||, ;, |, |&, & and newlines, and requires every subcommand to match independently.

lessons.title: File rules — the silent no-op
lessons.objective: Write a file permission rule that is actually consulted.
lessons.teach:
You want to stop Claude reading your .env. The obvious rule is wrong in a way that produces no error at the moment you need it.

File permission checks consult only Read(path) and Edit(path) rules. A path rule written for Write, NotebookEdit, Glob or the legacy MultiEdit is accepted, stored, and never consulted.

Claude Code warns at startup — but the file was still readable the whole time you thought it was protected.

IntentWrongRight
Block readsGlob(./secrets/**)Read(./secrets/**)
Block writesWrite(./secrets/**)Edit(./secrets/**)

Edit(path) governs all the built-in tools that write files, Write and NotebookEdit included. There is one rule form for reading and one for writing; that is the whole vocabulary.

Path anchors matter too. ./x is relative to the settings file. //x is absolute from the filesystem root — so Read(//Users/alice/secrets/**) means the real /Users/alice/secrets. A single leading slash anchors at the rule's source instead, which is rarely what you meant.

One more: output redirection is checked as a file write. A rule allowing git commit allows the command, not the target of a > in it. /dev/null is exempt; a target containing ~ or a glob always prompts.

example.label: Excluding secrets, correctly

lessons.takeaway: Only Read(path) and Edit(path) are consulted. Write/Glob/NotebookEdit path rules are accepted and ignored.

checks.q: You want to stop Claude reading .env files. Which rule works?
checks.why: File permission checks consult only Edit(path) and Read(path). The other three are accepted, warned about at startup, and never consulted — a rule that looks like protection and is not.

lessons.title: Permission modes
lessons.objective: Pick the right mode for a task and know what each stops auto-approving.
lessons.teach:
A mode sets the baseline for everything your rules do not explicitly cover. Switch with Shift+Tab in the CLI.

ModeWhat runs without asking
default (Manual)Read-only commands only. Everything else prompts.
planReads and read-only commands. Claude explores and proposes, never edits your source.
acceptEditsFile edits, plus mkdir, touch, mv, cp, sed in the working directory.
autoA classifier model reviews actions instead of you.
dontAskNothing new — anything not pre-approved is denied, not prompted.
bypassPermissionsAlmost everything, including writes to .git and .claude.

Two are worth extra attention.

dontAsk is the CI mode. It converts every prompt into a denial. That makes your tool surface fixed and explicit, which is exactly what you want when no human is watching.

plan is stronger than it looks. File edits are never auto-approved in plan mode, even when an allow rule matches. That is a deliberate exception to normal rule evaluation.

Regardless of mode, a short list is never auto-approved: anything matched by an explicit ask rule, tools that require user interaction like AskUserQuestion, and rm/rmdir targeting a critical path. There are also protected paths — .git, .vscode, .idea, .husky and friends — whose writes no allow rule can pre-approve; only bypassPermissions lets them through.

example.label: Locking the modes down org-wide

lessons.takeaway: dontAsk denies instead of prompting. plan never auto-approves edits, even with a matching allow rule.

checks.q: Which mode auto-DENIES anything not already pre-approved?
checks.why: dontAsk converts any permission prompt into a denial. Tools pre-approved by allow rules still run. It is the right posture for a headless agent where nobody can answer a prompt.

checks.q: In plan mode, an allow rule matches a file edit Claude wants to make. Does it run?
choices: No — plan mode never auto-approves file edits, even with a matching allow rule
Only if you are also in acceptEdits
Only for files inside the working directory
checks.why: Plan mode routes file edits and shell writes to a prompt regardless of allow rules, so write operations cannot be auto-approved while planning. It is a deliberate exception to normal evaluation.

lessons.title: Settings files, precedence and trust
lessons.objective: Predict which file wins, and explain why a cloned repo cannot silently widen your access.
lessons.teach:
Five sources hold settings. Highest precedence first:

  1. Managed — your organization. Nothing overrides it, not even a CLI flag.
  2. Command line — claude --settings
  3. Project local — .claude/settings.local.json (yours, gitignored)
  4. Shared project — .claude/settings.json (committed)
  5. User — ~/.claude/settings.json

Scalars override; lists merge. Set permissions.allow in three files and you get the union of all three. This is why “I removed that allow rule and it still applies” almost always means another scope still declares it.

Now the security question. A repository can ship a .claude/settings.json. Cloning it must not silently grant the author access to your machine. So Claude Code splits the file by direction:

RulesWhen they apply
deny and askImmediately
allow, additionalDirectories, most envOnly after you trust the folder

Restrictions bind at once; grants wait for a human. Learn this asymmetry — it answers a whole family of questions, and it is the principle behind several later lessons.

Last thing: settings files are strict JSON. A // comment or a trailing comma is a syntax error that surfaces as a Settings Error at your next start.

example.label: Which file for which job
example.code:
~/.claude/settings.json          your preferences, every project
.claude/settings.json            the team's rules — commit this
.claude/settings.local.json      your approvals here — gitignored
managed-settings.json            org policy — you cannot override it

lessons.takeaway: Managed > CLI > local > project > user. Lists merge. deny/ask apply at once; allow waits for trust.

checks.q: A teammate clones your repo with a committed .claude/settings.json. Which rules take effect BEFORE they trust the folder?
checks.why: Restrictions bind immediately; grants wait. deny and ask apply at once, while permissions.allow, additionalDirectories, extraKnownMarketplaces and most env values wait for the trust step. Otherwise cloning a repo would silently widen your access.

checks.q: You set permissions.allow in both your user settings and the project's settings.json. What happens?
choices: The higher-precedence file's list replaces the other
The lists merge — entries from both apply
Only the user file is read
checks.why: List keys such as permissions.allow merge across scopes rather than overriding, so each file can contribute entries. Scalar keys follow normal precedence.

title: Extending Claude Code
blurb: Four mechanisms — skills, hooks, subagents, MCP. Each solves a different problem, and choosing the wrong one is the most common mistake.

lessons.title: Choosing a mechanism
lessons.objective: Given a requirement, name which of the four extension points it belongs to.
lessons.teach:
Before the details, the decision. Four mechanisms, four different jobs:

You want…UseBecause
Claude to know a fact, alwaysCLAUDE.mdloaded every session
A repeatable procedure, on demandSkillloads only when invoked — costs nothing until used
Something to happen every time, guaranteedHookthe harness runs it as code; Claude cannot forget
Work done without polluting your contextSubagentseparate context window; returns a conclusion
Access to an external systemMCPconnects real tools and data

The two failure modes are worth naming now, because both are common:

Putting a procedure in CLAUDE.md. It works, but you pay its tokens on every turn of every session forever, and adherence drops as the file grows. If a section of your CLAUDE.md has become a numbered procedure rather than a fact, that is the signal to make it a skill.

Putting a guarantee in a prompt. “Always run the linter” in CLAUDE.md, in your prompt, or in a skill is a request. Only a hook is a guarantee. If the answer to “what if Claude doesn't?” is “that's a problem”, you need a hook.

example.label: The same requirement, three ways
example.code:
"We use pnpm, not npm"
  -> CLAUDE.md. A fact, always relevant, one line.

"Here is our 12-step release procedure"
  -> Skill. Long, only relevant when releasing, loads on demand.

"Never let a commit through without the linter passing"
  -> Hook. A guarantee. PostToolUse on Edit|Write, or PreToolUse on
     Bash(git commit *).

lessons.takeaway: Facts → CLAUDE.md. Procedures → skills. Guarantees → hooks. Context isolation → subagents. External systems → MCP.

checks.q: A section of your CLAUDE.md has grown into a numbered 12-step deployment procedure. What should you do?
choices: Leave it — CLAUDE.md is the right home for instructions
Move it to a skill, so it loads only when you invoke it
Split it across several CLAUDE.md files
checks.why: A skill's body loads only when used, so long reference material costs almost nothing until you need it. A CLAUDE.md section costs its tokens on every turn of every session. 'A section that has become a procedure rather than a fact' is the documented signal to convert it.

lessons.title: Skills
lessons.objective: Write a skill, and explain the two different lifetimes inside it.
lessons.teach:
A skill is a markdown file with YAML frontmatter that becomes a slash command. .claude/skills/deploy/SKILL.md gives you /deploy.

(Custom commands were merged into skills. A file at .claude/commands/deploy.md does the same thing and still works; the skill form adds a directory for supporting files and richer frontmatter.)

Claude can invoke a skill itself when it seems relevant — which you often do not want for anything with side effects. Hence:

disable-model-invocation: true   # only you can trigger it

Now the part that gets tested. A skill has two different lifetimes:

Lifetime
The skill's contentEnters the conversation once and stays for the whole session. Claude Code never re-reads the file.
Its allowed-tools grantApplies to the invoking turn only. Clears when you send your next message.

The practical consequence: write standing instructions, not one-time steps. “First, read the changelog” reads fine on turn one and badly on turn nine, because the text is still sitting there. Write “Always prefer X over Y” instead.

Arguments use $ARGUMENTS for the whole string, or $ARGUMENTS[N] / $N for one by index — 0-based, so $0 is the first argument. If you pass arguments and the body has no placeholder, Claude Code appends ARGUMENTS: your text so nothing is lost.

Security note. Workspace trust does not gate allowed-tools. A skill committed to a repository applies its grant whenever it is invoked — including in a -p run in a folder you have never trusted. Read the allowed-tools of repository skills before running Claude Code there.

example.label: A skill with a scoped, prompt-free grant
example.code:
---
name: commit
description: Stage and commit the current changes with a conventional message.
argument-hint: "[scope]"
disable-model-invocation: true
allowed-tools: Bash(git add *) Bash(git commit *) Bash(git status *)
---

Review the staged changes and commit them.

- Write a conventional-commit subject line, scoped to $ARGUMENTS if given.
- Never commit files the user did not stage.
- If nothing is staged, say so and stop — do not stage anything yourself.

lessons.takeaway: Skill content persists all session; its allowed-tools grant lasts one turn. $0 is the first argument.

checks.q: How long does a skill's allowed-tools grant last?
choices: Only the turn that invoked the skill — it clears at your next message
Until the skill is invoked again
checks.why: The grant covers the invoking turn and clears when you send your next message, even though the skill's CONTENT stays in context for the whole session. To pre-approve for a whole session, use permission settings instead.

checks.q: Your skill body says 'First, read the changelog.' On turn nine Claude reads it again unprompted. Why?
choices: The rendered skill content stays in the conversation for the session, so a one-time step reads as a standing instruction forever
checks.why: The rendered SKILL.md enters the conversation as one message and persists; Claude Code does not re-read the file on later turns. Write guidance as standing instructions rather than sequenced steps.

checks.q: In a skill body, what does $1 expand to?
checks.why: $N is shorthand for $ARGUMENTS[N] and indexing is 0-based, so $0 is first and $1 is second. Bare $ARGUMENTS is the whole string as typed.

lessons.title: Hooks — the guarantee mechanism
lessons.objective: Write a hook that blocks a tool call, and read its exit codes correctly.
lessons.teach:
A hook is code the harness runs at a fixed lifecycle point. That is the entire reason it exists: “please always run the linter” is a request Claude can forget; a PostToolUse hook cannot.

Configuration nests three levels: event → matcher group → handler.

The events you will actually use:

  • PreToolUse — before a call. Can block.
  • PostToolUse — after success. (Failures fire PostToolUseFailure.)
  • UserPromptSubmit — before Claude sees your prompt. Can block or rewrite it.
  • SessionStart / SessionEnd, PreCompact / PostCompact, SubagentStart / SubagentStop

Your hook receives the event as JSON on stdin and communicates back two ways.

Exit codes — three outcomes, and the third is the trap:

ExitMeaning
0Success. stdout is parsed as JSON for structured control.
2Blocking error. The call is stopped.
anything elseNon-blocking error — reported, and the action proceeds.

A hook with a typo that exits 1 does not fail loudly. It silently stops protecting you.

Structured JSON is the richer path — it lets you deny with a reason Claude can act on, or even rewrite the tool's input.

Matchers are worth one line of care: a matcher of only letters, digits, _, -, spaces, commas or pipes is an exact string or list (Edit|Write). Anything else is compiled as an unanchored JavaScript regex (^Notebook.*).

example.label: A PreToolUse hook that denies with a reason

lessons.takeaway: Exit 0 = success (JSON read), 2 = block, anything else = the action proceeds anyway.

checks.q: Your hook script has a typo and exits with status 1. Does the tool call still run?
choices: Yes — only 2 is a blocking error; every other non-zero code is non-blocking and the action proceeds
checks.why: Only 0 (success) and 2 (blocking error) are special. Every other exit code is a non-blocking error: it is reported, and the action proceeds. A broken hook silently stops protecting you — which is why you test hooks by piping JSON into them.

checks.q: Which JSON does a PreToolUse hook emit to deny a call with a reason?
checks.why: PreToolUse uses hookSpecificOutput with permissionDecision and permissionDecisionReason, and can also supply updatedInput to rewrite the call. The bare {decision, reason} shape belongs to the PermissionRequest event.

lessons.title: Hooks vs. rules — the precedence you must know
lessons.objective: Predict the outcome when a hook and a permission rule disagree, in both directions.
lessons.teach:
Hooks and permission rules both gate tool calls, so what happens when they disagree? The answer is asymmetric, and both halves are tested.

Direction 1 — a hook says allow, a deny rule matches.

Deny rule wins. The call is blocked.

Hook decisions do not bypass permission rules. Claude Code evaluates deny and ask rules regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returned. Deny-first precedence is preserved, including for deny rules from managed settings.

Direction 2 — a hook exits 2, an allow rule matches.

Hook wins. The call is blocked.

An exit-2 hook stops the call before permission rules are evaluated at all.

Read those together and the principle is clean: restrictions win in both directions. Nothing you configure can make a call run that something else wanted blocked.

And that asymmetry is what solves the problem from Lesson 5 — “allow all of X except Y”, which deny rules alone cannot express:

The pattern: put "Bash" in your allow list, then register a PreToolUse hook that rejects the specific cases. The allow rule handles the common path with no prompts; the hook, running first, catches the exceptions with the full expressive power of code rather than a glob.

example.label: Allow-with-exceptions

lessons.takeaway: Hook 'allow' loses to a deny rule; hook exit 2 beats an allow rule. Restrictions win in both directions.

checks.q: A PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision 'allow', but a project deny rule also matches. What happens?
choices: The hook wins and the call runs
The deny rule wins and the call is blocked
checks.why: Hook decisions do not bypass permission rules. Deny and ask rules are evaluated regardless of what a PreToolUse hook returns, preserving deny-first precedence.

checks.q: You want every Bash command to run without prompting EXCEPT a handful you consider dangerous. What is the documented approach?
choices: Add 'Bash' to allow, and a PreToolUse hook that exits 2 for the dangerous cases
Add 'Bash' to allow plus narrower deny rules — allow wins for everything else
Use bypassPermissions with a PostToolUse hook
Not possible — allow and deny cannot combine on one tool
checks.why: A hook exiting 2 stops the call before permission rules are evaluated, so it overrides the allow rule. Deny rules cannot do this, because a deny rule cannot carry allowlist exceptions — a broad deny blocks everything it matches.

lessons.title: Subagents
lessons.objective: Say what a subagent does and does not receive, and when the handoff is worth it.
lessons.teach:
A subagent is a specialized assistant with its own context window. You reach for one for two reasons: a task produces output you do not want in your main conversation, or you want to hard-limit what a piece of work can touch.

Defined as markdown with frontmatter in .claude/agents/. Only name and description are required.

The constraint is structural, not persuasive. Setting tools: Read, Grep, Glob removes the write tools from the agent's pool entirely. A confused agent, a bad prompt, or injected text in a file it reads cannot make it write. That is a different kind of guarantee from asking it nicely.

What crosses the boundary matters:

ReceivesDoes not receive
Its own system promptThe main conversation history
The task message Claude writes for itOutput style preferences
CLAUDE.md (except Explore/Plan)Auto memory from the main session
A git status snapshotSkills invoked earlier in the main session

A subagent cannot call AskUserQuestion — it is removed, along with EndConversation, plan-mode tools and Workflow. So design its prompt to resolve its own ambiguity, or to report both readings and let the main session decide. It cannot stop and ask.

@-mention guarantees a specific subagent runs; relying on the description means Claude decides. model defaults to inherit — routing verbose mechanical work to a faster model is a real cost lever.

And when not to: a subagent starting from a blank context has to rediscover what you already know. For a small edit in a file you are looking at, the handoff costs more than it saves.

example.label: An agent that cannot write, by construction
example.code:
---
name: notes-auditor
description: Audit the notes in docs/ against the code and report drift.
             Use when asked whether documentation is still accurate.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
model: inherit
---

You audit documentation against the code it describes.

Report only — you have no write tools and must not ask for them.
Proposing an edit is the main session's job, not yours.

For each finding give file:line for both sides, then your judgement of
which is correct. If you find nothing, say so in one sentence.

lessons.takeaway: Own context window, no conversation history, cannot ask questions. Tool limits are structural, not advisory.

checks.q: Your subagent needs to ask the user which of two readings they meant. How does it do that?
choices: It cannot — that tool is removed from every subagent; design the prompt to resolve or report both readings
By returning a special exit code
checks.why: AskUserQuestion is removed from every subagent, along with EndConversation, the plan-mode tools, ScheduleWakeup and Workflow. A subagent's prompt must resolve its own ambiguity or report both options for the main session to decide.

checks.q: What does a non-fork subagent NOT receive?
choices: Skills previously invoked in the main session
checks.why: It gets a fresh context: its own system prompt, the task message, CLAUDE.md (except Explore and Plan), a git status snapshot, and any preloaded skills. It does not get the main conversation history, output style, auto memory, or skills invoked earlier. A fork is the variant that DOES inherit the full history.

lessons.title: MCP
lessons.objective: Add a server, name its tools in a rule, and explain the approval asymmetry.
lessons.teach:
MCP — the Model Context Protocol — is an open standard for connecting Claude to external systems. Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from somewhere else.

Four transports, added four ways:

claude mcp add --transport http  notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
claude mcp add --transport sse    asana https://mcp.asana.com/sse
claude mcp add --transport stdio  local -- npx -y my-server
claude mcp add-json events '{"type":"ws","url":"wss://…"}'

For stdio servers the bare -- separates Claude's own flags from the server's command line; everything after it is passed through untouched. (--transport does not accept ws — WebSocket servers must go through add-json or .mcp.json.)

Tools are named mcp__<server>__<tool> — mcp__github__get_issue. That naming is what permission rules and hook matchers must use. And allow globs need a literal, glob-free server segment: mcp__github__get_* works, mcp__* is skipped with a warning and approves nothing.

Three scopes: local (default, private to you), project (writes .mcp.json at the repo root, meant to be committed), and user (all your projects).

The asymmetry that matters. Project-scoped servers from .mcp.json prompt for approval in interactive sessions. claude -p, Agent SDK sessions and cloud sessions cannot show that prompt, so they load them without asking.

Read that twice. A .mcp.json in a repo you cloned is a request to run someone else's code, and CI is exactly the place where nobody sees the prompt. To exclude a server regardless of mode, use disabledMcpjsonServers.

example.label: Project config and a matching allow rule

lessons.takeaway: mcp__server__tool naming. Project servers prompt interactively but load silently under -p, the SDK and cloud.

checks.q: A repo contains .mcp.json. In which contexts do those servers load WITHOUT an approval prompt?
checks.why: Interactive sessions prompt before using project-scoped servers. Non-interactive contexts cannot show that prompt, so they load them without asking — which is why a .mcp.json from an untrusted repo is a real supply-chain concern in CI.

checks.q: Which MCP allow rule actually auto-approves tools?
checks.why: Allow rules accept tool-name globs only after a literal mcp__<server>__ prefix, and the server segment must be glob-free. Unanchored globs are skipped with a warning and approve nothing.

title: Running it without you
blurb: Headless runs, CI, and the security posture that changes the moment no human is watching a prompt.

lessons.title: Headless mode
lessons.objective: Run Claude Code from a script and consume its structured output.
lessons.teach:
Add -p (or --print) and Claude Code runs non-interactively: prompt in, result out, exit.

claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit"

It behaves like a Unix tool. stdin is read (capped at 10MB), exit code 0 on success and non-zero on failure, so scripts can branch on it.

Output formats:

--output-formatGives you
text (default)plain text
jsonresult, session_id, usage, total_cost_usd
stream-jsonnewline-delimited events; the last line is the result

Add --json-schema to constrain the answer; it arrives in structured_output.

Sessions persist across invocations, so a script can hold a conversation:

id=$(claude -p "Start a review" --output-format json | jq -r '.session_id')
claude -p "Now check the database queries" --resume "$id"

One quiet failure mode to know now: a plugin or MCP server that fails to load does not fail the run. The system/init event carries plugin_errors and mcp_server_errors; a CI gate has to check them itself.

example.label: Claude as a linter in package.json

lessons.takeaway: -p makes Claude Code a Unix tool. json/stream-json give you structured output; load errors do not fail the run.

checks.q: Your CI run passes --mcp-config and one server fails validation. What happens?
choices: The run aborts with a non-zero exit
The server is skipped, the run continues and exits cleanly — check mcp_server_errors yourself
The server is retried until it connects
checks.why: Invalid entries are skipped and the run continues and exits cleanly. The system/init event carries mcp_servers/mcp_server_errors and plugins/plugin_errors, and a CI gate must fail on a non-empty errors array itself. When a CI runner captures stderr, no warning is printed at all.

lessons.title: Why CI needs --bare
lessons.objective: Explain the specific risk of a non-bare -p run and write a hardened command.
lessons.teach:
This lesson is one fact, and it is the most security-relevant thing in the course.

Without --bare, a claude -p run executes the hooks in a project's .claude/settings.json and connects the servers in its .mcp.json — in a folder you have never trusted, with no workspace-trust dialog and no per-server approval prompt.

Now recall Lesson 9: deny and ask bind immediately, but allow waits for trust. That protection depends on a human being able to grant trust. Under -p, trust verification is disabled — because there is no way to show the dialog.

Put those together and think about CI running against a pull request from a fork. The attacker controls .claude/settings.json and .mcp.json in that branch.

--bare is the answer. It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, commands, subagents, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md. It is the recommended mode for scripted and SDK calls, and is slated to become the default for -p.

One consequence: in bare mode Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the system keychain. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. (Bedrock, Google Cloud and Foundry still read their own provider credentials.)

The rest of a hardened run:

  • -p starts in Manual mode on every plan — so pin the mode. --permission-mode dontAsk denies rather than prompting.
  • Narrow the tools. Better still, pipe the input in so the run needs no Bash permission at all to see it.
  • Cap the blast radius: --max-turns, --max-budget-usd.

example.label: A run you could point at an untrusted PR
example.code:
git diff main | claude \
  --bare \
  -p "Review this diff for correctness bugs. Report file:line and one line each." \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --allowedTools "Read" \
  --max-turns 12 \
  --max-budget-usd 2 \
  --output-format json

# --bare      repo config does not execute
# dontAsk     anything unlisted is denied, not queued for a prompt nobody sees
# piped diff  no Bash permission needed to read the change
# caps        a runaway loop cannot spend your afternoon

lessons.takeaway: Without --bare, a -p run executes untrusted repo hooks and MCP servers, and trust verification is off under -p.

checks.q: Which safeguard is explicitly DISABLED when running with -p?
choices: Trust verification for first-time codebases and new MCP servers
checks.why: Trust verification is disabled non-interactively because the dialog cannot be shown. Combined with a non-bare run executing the repo's hooks and .mcp.json servers, that is exactly why --bare is the correct default for CI.

checks.q: You add --bare and authentication now fails, though you are logged in interactively. Why?
choices: In bare mode Claude Code never reads OAuth credentials or the keychain — set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
Bare mode only works on Bedrock
checks.why: Bare mode does not use your subscription login. Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or supply an apiKeyHelper in --settings JSON. Bedrock, Google Cloud and Foundry continue reading their own provider credentials.

lessons.title: Context at scale
lessons.objective: Predict what survives compaction and choose the right tool to keep a long session healthy.
lessons.teach:
Long sessions fill the window, and Claude Code compacts: it summarizes the conversation history to fit. What happens to your carefully placed instructions depends entirely on how they were loaded.

MechanismAfter compaction
System prompt and output styleUnchanged — never part of message history
Project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rulesRe-injected from disk
Auto memoryRe-injected from disk
Rules with paths: frontmatterLost until a matching file is read again
Nested CLAUDE.md in subdirectoriesLost until a file there is read again
Invoked skill bodiesRe-injected — capped at 5,000 tokens per skill, 25,000 total, oldest dropped first
HooksN/A — hooks are code, not context

Two things follow that you can act on:

If a rule must survive compaction, drop its paths: frontmatter or move it to the project-root CLAUDE.md. Path-scoped rules enter message history when their trigger file is read, so compaction summarizes them away like anything else.

Skill truncation keeps the START of the file. Put the load-bearing instructions near the top of SKILL.md, never in a closing section.

The levers, roughly in order of how much they buy you:

  • Subagents — the structural fix. Reading happens in another window.
  • Skills — bodies load on demand, so reference material is free until used.
  • Tool search — MCP schemas stay deferred; only names load at startup.
  • /context to diagnose, /compact to continue, /clear when the task changed.

example.label: A rule that survives, and one that does not
example.code:
<!-- .claude/rules/api.md — LOST after compaction until a match is read -->
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---
All API endpoints must validate input.

<!-- .claude/rules/always.md — no paths: field, so re-injected from disk -->
Never write to the balances table directly; go through src/ledger/.

lessons.takeaway: Path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md are lost to compaction; project-root CLAUDE.md and auto memory are re-injected.

checks.q: After a /compact, which of these is LOST until its trigger fires again?
checks.why: Project-root CLAUDE.md, unscoped rules and auto memory are re-injected from disk. The system prompt is never in message history. Path-scoped rules and nested CLAUDE.md entered message history when their trigger file was read, so compaction summarizes them away.

checks.q: Where should the most important instructions go in a long SKILL.md, and why?
choices: At the end, so they are read last
Near the top — compaction truncates skill bodies from the start, keeping the beginning
checks.why: Skill bodies are re-injected after compaction but truncated to a 5,000-token per-skill cap, and truncation keeps the START of the file. Anything in a closing section is what gets dropped.

title: The API and the SDKs
blurb: Claude Code is one way to use Claude. The exam also covers calling the API directly and building agents on it.

lessons.title: The Messages API
lessons.objective: Read a response correctly and handle the stop reasons that matter.
lessons.teach:
Everything goes through one endpoint: POST /v1/messages. Tool use, extended thinking, caching and structured outputs are all features of that endpoint, not separate APIs.

The API is stateless — you resend the full conversation every time. That single fact is why caching and context management matter as much as they do.

The first bug everyone writes is response.content[0].text. content is a list of blocks — thinking, text, tool_use — and with thinking on, block 0 is usually a thinking block. Iterate and check block.type.

Stop reasons you must handle:

end_turnfinished naturally
tool_useexecute the tool and continue the loop
max_tokenstruncated mid-thought — you pay for the retry too
pause_turna server-side tool paused; resend to resume. Looks like an ending and is not.
refusala safety decline. Arrives as HTTP 200, not an exception.

Two current-generation details that catch people out: prefill is removed (seeding the assistant turn returns a 400 — use structured outputs instead), and effort lives inside output_config, not at the top level.

example.label: A correct first call
example.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    system="You are a concise technical writer.",
    thinking={"type": "adaptive"},        # not budget_tokens — that is a 400 now
    output_config={"effort": "medium"},   # inside output_config, not top level
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain MCP transports briefly."}],
)

if response.stop_reason == "refusal":     # HTTP 200, not an exception
    raise SystemExit(response.stop_details.category)

for block in response.content:            # a LIST of blocks
    if block.type == "text":
        print(block.text)

lessons.takeaway: One endpoint, stateless, content is a list of blocks. refusal is a 200; pause_turn is not an ending.

checks.q: Why is response.content[0].text a common bug?
choices: content is a string, not a list
content is a LIST of blocks — with thinking on, block 0 is usually a thinking block
The field is called message, not text
content is only populated when streaming
checks.why: response.content is a list of content block objects: thinking, text, tool_use. Iterate and check block.type before reading .text.

checks.q: Which stop_reason looks like an ending but is not?
checks.why: pause_turn means a server-side tool hit an iteration limit and the turn can be resumed by sending the paused assistant content back. Treating it as terminal gives you a silently truncated answer with no error and no warning.

lessons.title: Tool use and the agent loop
lessons.objective: Write the agentic loop correctly, including the mistake that degrades it silently.
lessons.teach:
You define tools; Claude asks to call them; you execute and send results back; repeat until it stops asking. That loop is an agent.

A tool is a name, a description and a JSON Schema. The description is the highest-leverage field — and the trick is to be prescriptive about when to call it, not just what it does. Recent models reach for tools conservatively, so “Call this when the user asks about current prices” measurably raises the should-call rate over “Gets prices”.

The silent degradation. When Claude returns three tool_use blocks in one message, all three tool_result blocks go back in a single user message. Splitting them across several messages does not error — it quietly trains Claude to stop making parallel calls, and your agent gets slower over the conversation for no visible reason.

A failed tool still gets a tool_result, with is_error: true. Dropping it leaves an unanswered tool_use and the next request is rejected.

More generally: return errors as tool results, not as exceptions. An uncaught exception aborts the run and the model never learns the tool failed. Returning "error: no records found, ask the user to widen the date range" turns a crash into a conversation.

example.label: The loop, and the one-message rule

lessons.takeaway: All parallel tool_results go back in one user message. Return tool errors as results, never as exceptions.

checks.q: Claude returns three tool_use blocks in one message. How do you return the results?
choices: One user message per result, in order
All three tool_result blocks in a single user message
checks.why: Splitting them across several messages silently trains Claude to stop making parallel calls — no error, just a gradually more sequential agent. A failed tool still gets a tool_result with is_error: true.

lessons.title: Prompt caching
lessons.objective: Lay out a request so the cache hits, and diagnose it when it does not.
lessons.teach:
Caching can cut the cost of a large repeated prefix by up to about 90%. It is also the feature most often silently broken.

Caching is a prefix match.

Render order is tools → system → messages. Any byte change anywhere in the cached prefix invalidates everything after it. So: stable content first, volatile content after the last breakpoint.

Verify, never assume. If usage.cache_read_input_tokens is zero across repeated identical-prefix requests, something is invalidating it:

InvalidatorFix
datetime.now() or a UUID in the system promptmove it after the breakpoint
json.dumps() on an unsorted dictsort_keys=True
A tool list built from a setsort it
A prefix under ~1024 tokenstoo short to cache at all

Economics: writes cost about 1.25×, reads about 0.1×. Max 4 breakpoints. That asymmetry is why a prefix that gets rewritten every turn is worse than not caching at all.

Three agent-specific workarounds worth memorizing, because each looks harmless and is not:

  • Editing the system prompt mid-session invalidates the cache → append a {"role": "system"} message to messages[] instead.
  • Switching models mid-session invalidates it → spawn a subagent on the cheaper model and keep the main loop on one model.
  • Adding or removing tools invalidates it → use tool search, which appends schemas rather than swapping them.

example.label: Stable first, volatile last
example.code:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5",
    max_tokens=16000,
    system=[{
        "type": "text",
        "text": BIG_STABLE_CONTEXT,               # never changes between calls
        "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"},   # <- the breakpoint
    }],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": todays_question}],  # volatile, after it
)

print(response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens)   # 0 means something broke it

lessons.takeaway: Prefix match, tools→system→messages. Stable first. Verify with cache_read_input_tokens.

checks.q: Where should volatile content — a timestamp, the user's question — go?
choices: At the very start so the model sees it first
Anywhere — the cache keys on content, not position
checks.why: Render order is tools, then system, then messages, and any byte change in the cached prefix invalidates everything after it. Stable content goes first; volatile content goes after the last breakpoint.

checks.q: cache_read_input_tokens is zero across repeated requests with what should be an identical prefix. Which are plausible causes?
choices: A datetime.now() or UUID in the system prompt
A tool list built from a set, so its order varies
Using the same model on every request
checks.why: Those are the classic silent invalidators, plus a prefix under ~1024 tokens which never caches at all. Keeping the model constant HELPS — switching models mid-session is itself an invalidator.

lessons.title: Four ways to build an agent
lessons.objective: Distinguish the Tool Runner, the Claude Agent SDK, and Managed Agents.
lessons.teach:
Two independent questions separate the options: who supplies the harness (the loop and context management), and who supplies the deployment (the infrastructure it runs on).

ApproachYou writeHarness / deployment
Manual loopthe while loop yourselfyou build it, you host it
Tool Runner
client.beta.messages.tool_runner		just the tool functionsSDK harness, you host
Claude Agent SDK
claude-agent-sdk		a prompt + optionsClaude Code harness, you host
Managed Agentsan agent configAnthropic harness and hosted sandbox

Tool Runner ≠ Claude Agent SDK. They sound alike and are different packages. Tool Runner lives in the regular Anthropic API SDK and is a thin helper over POST /v1/messages that loops over tools you define — no built-in tools, no filesystem, no sandbox. The Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code packaged as a library: built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash, subagents, hooks, permissions, sessions.

Both are harness-only — you host and deploy them. Only Managed Agents adds managed deployment.

Before choosing the agent tier at all, the docs give four criteria: complexity (multi-step and hard to specify up front?), value (does it justify the cost and latency?), viability (is Claude good at this?), and cost of error (can mistakes be caught?). Any “no” means drop to a scripted workflow or a single call. Most production LLM work is a single call.

example.label: Tool Runner: you write tools, not loops
example.code:
from anthropic import Anthropic, beta_tool

@beta_tool
def get_weather(location: str, unit: str = "celsius") -> str:
    """Get current weather for a location.

    Call this when the user asks about weather, temperature or conditions.

    Args:
        location: City and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA.
        unit: Either "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
    """
    return f"18C and raining in {location}"

runner = Anthropic().beta.messages.tool_runner(
    model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=16000,
    tools=[get_weather],
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Weather in Paris?"}],
)
for message in runner:      # the SDK drives the loop
    print(message)

# The docstring IS the tool description. The Args: block IS the schema.

lessons.takeaway: Tool Runner = API SDK helper, your tools only. Agent SDK = Claude Code as a library. Only Managed Agents hosts it too.

checks.q: What is the difference between the SDK's Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK?
choices: Two names for the same package
Tool Runner is a helper in the Anthropic API SDK that loops over tools YOU define; the Claude Agent SDK is a separate package shipping the Claude Code harness with built-in file and bash tools
Tool Runner is hosted by Anthropic; the Agent SDK runs locally
Tool Runner is Python-only; the Agent SDK is TypeScript-only
checks.why: Tool Runner is a thin helper over POST /v1/messages with no built-in tools and no sandbox. The Claude Agent SDK is Claude Code as a library. Both are harness-only — you host and deploy them; only Managed Agents adds managed deployment.

checks.q: Which approach gives you BOTH a managed agent loop and Anthropic-hosted infrastructure?
checks.why: The manual loop supplies neither; Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK supply a harness but you still host it. Only Managed Agents supplies both — Anthropic runs the loop and hosts a per-session sandbox.

lessons.title: The Agent SDK's permission flow
lessons.objective: Order the six steps and avoid the two traps that silently disable your checks.
lessons.teach:
The Agent SDK's evaluation order is richer than the CLI's deny→ask→allow, and the extra steps are where the traps live.

  1. Hooks — run first. Can deny outright. A hook returning allow does not skip steps 2 and 3.
  2. Deny rules — block even in bypassPermissions.
  3. Ask rules — fall through to your callback, even in bypassPermissions.
  4. Permission mode — bypassPermissions approves; plan routes edits to the callback regardless of allow rules.
  5. Allow rules — approve if matched.
  6. can_use_tool callback — only if nothing above resolved it. Skipped entirely in dontAsk, which denies instead.

Trap 1: auto-approved tools never reach can_use_tool. A security check in your callback is silently bypassed for anything an allow rule, acceptEdits or bypassPermissions already approved. A bare entry like allowed_tools=["Read"] auto-approves every Read. For a check that must run on every call, use a PreToolUse hook — hooks run before every other step.

Trap 2: allowed_tools does not constrain bypassPermissions. Unlisted tools are simply unmatched by an allow rule, so they fall through to the mode — which approves them. allowed_tools=["Read"] with bypassPermissions still permits Bash, Write and Edit. To block specific tools under bypass, use disallowed_tools.

For a genuinely locked-down agent, pair them the other way: allowed_tools=[…] with permission_mode="dontAsk".

example.label: Locked down, and the trap beside it
example.code:
# CORRECT: explicit surface, everything else denied outright
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Glob", "Grep"],
    permission_mode="dontAsk",
)

# TRAP: this approves EVERY tool, including Bash, Write and Edit.
options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read"],
    permission_mode="bypassPermissions",   # unlisted tools fall through to the mode
)

lessons.takeaway: Hooks → deny → ask → mode → allow → callback. Auto-approved tools skip the callback; allowed_tools does not constrain bypass.

checks.q: Put the Agent SDK's permission evaluation steps in order.
choices: Deny, ask, allow, hooks, mode, canUseTool
Hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, canUseTool
canUseTool, hooks, deny, ask, allow, mode
Permission mode, hooks, deny, ask, allow, canUseTool
checks.why: Hooks run first and can deny outright, but a hook returning allow does not skip the deny and ask rules below it. The callback is last, and is skipped entirely in dontAsk mode.

checks.q: You put a security check in can_use_tool and set allowed_tools=['Read']. Why might the check never run for Read?
choices: Auto-approved tools never reach the callback — a bare allow entry approves every call to that tool first
Read is read-only and exempt from checks
The callback must be registered before allowed_tools
checks.why: Anything approved at an earlier step skips the callback. A bare name like 'Read' auto-approves every Read; a scoped rule like Bash(ls *) only auto-approves matching calls. Use a PreToolUse hook for a check that must run on every call.

lessons.title: Untrusted content and the sandbox
lessons.objective: Name the injection surfaces and say what the Bash sandbox does that permissions cannot.
lessons.teach:
The last idea, and the one that ties the course together.

Everything the model reads is untrusted. Issue bodies, PR review comments, CI logs, web pages, MCP tool output, files in a repo you cloned. All of it is attacker-influenceable, and all of it must be treated as data, never as instructions.

Claude Code's own defences are worth knowing by name: the permission system; context-aware analysis; network commands like curl and wget are not auto-approved; WebFetch runs in an isolated context window specifically so fetched content cannot inject into your conversation; trust verification; command-injection detection even for previously allowlisted commands; and fail-closed matching.

But permissions have a structural limit. They are evaluated before a command runs, from the command string. They cannot know what a command will actually do.

That is what the sandbox adds.

ControlsEnforced
Permission ruleswhether a call runsbefore it, from the command string
Sandboxwhat a Bash command can accessby the OS, on the running process

So the sandbox holds regardless of what the model chose to run, and even if an allowed command does more than its name suggests. macOS uses Seatbelt, Linux and WSL2 use bubblewrap. It covers Bash and its children only — Read, Edit and Write go through the permission system instead.

One rule to carry: in sandbox filesystem policy, a deny holds inside a wider allow, and a narrow allow re-opens a denied region. So allowRead: ["~/"] with denyRead: ["~/.env"] gives you the home directory without the secret — a broad allow cannot silently re-expose it.

And the honest caveat: by default the network proxy does not inspect TLS, so allowing a broad domain like github.com still creates an exfiltration path.

example.label: A policy your credentials survive

lessons.takeaway: Permissions gate whether a call runs, from its text. The sandbox gates what it can touch, enforced by the OS.

checks.q: What is the essential difference between a permission rule and the Bash sandbox?
choices: None — the sandbox is a permission mode
Permission rules decide whether a call runs, evaluated beforehand from the command string; the sandbox restricts what a running command can access, enforced by the OS on the process
Permission rules are OS-enforced; the sandbox is advisory
The sandbox covers every tool; permission rules cover only Bash
checks.why: Permission rules are evaluated before a tool runs and apply to every tool. The sandbox is OS-level enforcement on the running process and applies only to Bash and its children — so it holds regardless of what the model chose to run.

checks.q: Sandbox filesystem policy has allowRead: ['~/'] and denyRead: ['~/.env']. What is readable?
choices: Everything under home, including ~/.env — the broader allow wins
Everything under home except ~/.env — a deny holds inside a wider allow
checks.why: A deny holds inside a wider allow, so a broad allow cannot silently re-expose a secret. The reverse also works: denyRead ~/ with allowRead ~/projects re-opens that narrower region.

checks.q: Why does WebFetch use a separate context window?
choices: To avoid injecting potentially malicious fetched content into the main conversation
checks.why: Isolated context windows for web fetch are a named prompt-injection safeguard: fetched content is analyzed separately rather than dropped into the main conversation where it could act as instructions.
